details:
VIMOD — Satellite Hotspot Monitoring and Wildfire Prevention

VIMOD, developed by the HackerMonkeys team for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, is an interactive web platform designed to support wildfire prevention and environmental monitoring in Costa Rica and the world using satellite data from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments.

Our platform processes over 152,000 satellite hotspot detections collected between 2000 and 2026, transforming complex information into accessible visualizations and insights.

How Does It Work?

VIMOD combines four main features:

  • Interactive Hotspot Map: Displays satellite detections with geographic locations, dates, coordinates, and Fire Radiative Power (FRP), using colors to represent different levels of radiative intensity.
  • Geographic Dashboards: Identifies provinces and cantons with the highest concentrations of satellite hotspot detections.
  • Seasonal Trend Analysis: Detects recurring patterns across multiple years. For example, if hotspots repeatedly appear in Tilarán during February, VIMOD highlights this pattern to support preparedness planning.
  • Data-Driven Chatbot: Allows users to ask questions about historical detections, locations, and trends without relying on artificial intelligence.

Technologies Used

We developed VIMOD using Python, Streamlit, Pandas, Folium, Plotly, Shapely, Geopy, HTML, and CSS. We also used NASA satellite datasets, geographic boundary data, Jupyter Notebook for data preparation, and GitHub for version control.

The application is hosted using Streamlit Community Cloud, making it accessible through a web browser without specialized hardware.

Innovation and Impact

What makes VIMOD unique is its focus on turning historical satellite data into actionable wildfire preparedness insights.

Rather than simply showing where thermal anomalies have occurred, VIMOD identifies geographic and seasonal patterns that may help authorities prioritize monitoring, allocate resources, and prepare for periods of recurring activity.

During development, we prioritized scientific accuracy, accessibility, performance, cost-effectiveness, and the differences between MODIS and VIIRS observations.
